blocks.text: On a 24-hour clock, 5 hours after 22:00 is 03:00 rather than 27:00, because the count wraps back to 0 every 24 hours. Modular arithmetic applies the same wrap-around rule to any positive integer n, called the modulus. Dividing any integer a by n produces a unique integer quotient q and an integer remainder r satisfying a = q × n + r with 0 ≤ r < n. That remainder r is written a mod n. Even when a is negative, r stays between 0 and n − 1: for example, −3 = (−1) × 7 + 4, so (−3) mod 7 = 4. Figure 1 shows the remainders 0 to 6 arranged in a clockwise cycle for modulus 7: adding 1 steps one place clockwise, so 6 wraps around to 0.

blocks.text: Two integers a and b are called congruent modulo n, written a ≡ b (mod n), when they leave the same remainder on division by n. Equivalently, their difference is an integer multiple of n:
a ≡ b (mod n)   means   a − b = k × n   for some integer k
A major shortcut of modular arithmetic is that numbers can be replaced by their remainders before adding, subtracting or multiplying. If a ≡ c (mod n) and b ≡ d (mod n), then:
a + b ≡ c + d (mod n)   and   a × b ≡ c × d (mod n)

Applying the multiplication rule repeatedly also simplifies powers: if a^m ≡ 1 (mod n), every block of m factors of a contributes 1. Division, however, needs care: cancelling a factor that shares a common divisor greater than 1 with n does not keep the same modulus n. For instance, 2 × 4 = 8 and 2 × 1 = 2 both leave remainder 2 modulo 6, so 2 × 4 ≡ 2 × 1 (mod 6), yet 4 is not congruent to 1 modulo 6.

blocks.text: Electrical noise in cables and memory chips can flip a binary digit (bit), turning a 0 into a 1 or a 1 into a 0. The simplest safeguard attaches one extra check bit, called a parity bit, to every block of d data bits, sending a codeword of d + 1 bits. Under even parity, the sender chooses the parity bit (0 or 1) so that the total count of 1s across all d + 1 bits, including the parity bit itself, is even. Under odd parity, the parity bit makes the total count of 1s across all d + 1 bits odd.

When the receiver checks a codeword, any single-bit flip (whether in a data bit or in the parity bit) changes the count of 1s by +1 or −1, switching it between even and odd, so the error is detected. More generally, a single parity bit detects every odd number of bit flips, yet misses every even number of flips: flipping two bits changes the count of 1s by −2, 0 or +2, leaving its evenness or oddness intact. Even when an error is detected, a single parity bit cannot tell which bit flipped, so the receiver cannot correct the block on its own.

Arranging r × c data bits into r rows and c columns overcomes this limit. In a two-dimensional parity grid, one parity bit is appended to each of the r rows, one parity bit is placed at the foot of each of the c columns, and one corner parity bit at the bottom right checks the parity row and parity column:
transmitted bits = (r + 1) × (c + 1) = r × c + (r + c + 1)

If a single bit anywhere in the (r + 1) × (c + 1) grid flips, both its row and its column fail their parity checks, and their intersection pinpoints the exact bit to flip back. Any two-bit error also makes at least two row or column checks fail, so every two-bit error is detected, though not uniquely fixable; four flips sitting at the four corners of a rectangle, however, put two flips in each affected row and column and slip past unnoticed. blocks.text: Light travels fastest in a vacuum, at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ metres per second (m/s). In any transparent substance it travels at a slower speed v. The refractive index n of that substance is the dimensionless ratio of the two speeds, so n is at least 1:
n = c ÷ v

When a ray of light crosses a flat boundary between medium 1 (index n₁) and medium 2 (index n₂), this speed change usually bends the ray, an effect called refraction. In optics, angles are always measured between each ray and the normal, the dashed line drawn at 90° to the boundary in Figure 1, never to the boundary surface itself; a ray making angle α with the boundary therefore has angle 90° − α to the normal. Snell’s law links the angle of incidence θ₁ and the angle of refraction θ₂:
n₁ × sin θ₁ = n₂ × sin θ₂

An incident ray in Medium 1 meets the boundary at angle θ₁ to the normal, and the refracted ray in Medium 2 bends closer to the normal at smaller angle θ₂.

blocks.text: When light travels from a higher-index medium toward a lower-index one (n₁ > n₂), raising θ₁ eventually brings θ₂ to 90° (sin 90° = 1.00), so the refracted ray skims the boundary. That incident angle is the critical angle θ_c:
sin θ_c = n₂ ÷ n₁   (only when n₁ > n₂)

For any incident angle θ₁ > θ_c, Snell’s law would require sin θ₂ > 1, which is impossible: no light refracts across, and all of it reflects back into medium 1 (total internal reflection), the principle that keeps light inside the higher-index core of optical fibres.

blocks.text: When one face of a flat wall is kept at a warm temperature T_hot and the opposite face at a cooler temperature T_cold, thermal energy conducts through the solid from the warm face to the cool face. Once temperatures at every depth stop changing with time, conduction is in steady state: thermal energy enters the warm face and leaves the cool face at the same constant rate P, measured in watts (1 W = 1 joule per second; 1 kW = 1,000 W).
For one-dimensional steady conduction across a uniform slab of face area A (in m²) and thickness L (in m), Fourier’s law gives:
P = (k × A × (T_hot − T_cold)) ÷ L

Here k is the material’s thermal conductivity, in W/(m·K). Because a temperature difference of 1 °C equals 1 K, T_hot − T_cold gives the same number in °C and in K. Table 1 gives k for four building and engineering materials; metals conduct readily, whereas porous materials such as cork have tiny values of k and act as insulators.

blocks.text: To analyse insulated walls, engineers define a layer’s unit-area thermal resistance R, measured in (m²·K)/W:
R = L ÷ k   so that   P = (A × (T_hot − T_cold)) ÷ R

When flat layers of equal area A sit side by side in series (with negligible resistance at the joint), steady state requires the exact same heat-transfer rate P to pass through every layer, while their temperature drops add up to T_hot − T_cold. Consequently, their unit-area thermal resistances add:
R_total = R₁ + R₂ + … = (L₁ ÷ k₁) + (L₂ ÷ k₂) + …
Because ΔT_i = (P ÷ A) × R_i across layer i, each layer takes a share of the total temperature drop proportional to its own R_i. Figure 1 shows a two-layer exterior wall.

blocks.text: Manufacturers often have to decide whether to produce a part in-house (make) or purchase it from an outside supplier (buy, or outsource). Accounting reports usually group all factory costs together, yet not every cost in those reports changes when production stops. To compare making with buying accurately, management isolates relevant costs: future costs and benefits that differ between the two choices.

Two categories of cost do not differ between the choices and must be left out of the comparison. First, a sunk cost is money already spent in the past that cannot be recovered, such as the historical purchase price of specialised equipment with zero scrap or resale value. Second, an unavoidable fixed cost, such as an allocated share of factory-wide building rent or head-office salaries, continues in full even if the component is outsourced. By contrast, unit variable costs v (direct materials, direct labour and variable overhead) and avoidable fixed costs F_a (such as a dedicated tooling lease or supervisor contract cancelled upon outsourcing) stop when buying outside, so both are relevant.
For an annual requirement of q units, when the workshop space has no alternative use and an outside supplier quotes unit price p_b, the relevant annual outlays are:
relevant cost of making = F_a + v × q   versus   relevant cost of buying = p_b × q
When p_b > v, each unit made in-house saves p_b − v in variable outlay towards covering F_a, so the two options cost the same at the indifference volume q*:
q* = F_a ÷ (p_b − v)

Below q* units buying is cheaper; above q* units making is cheaper. If outsourcing also frees workshop space that can be rented out or used to earn net income R_alt, that opportunity benefit reduces the net cost of buying to p_b × q − R_alt:
net cost of buying with alternative space income = p_b × q − R_alt

blocks.text: Average income tells how much an economy earns per household, not how that total is shared. To picture the distribution of income, economists rank all households from lowest to highest income and often group them into equal slices, such as quarters (25% each) or quintiles (five groups of 20% each). Adding each group's share of total income from the bottom upwards gives the cumulative income share.

A Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentage of total income on the vertical axis against the cumulative percentage of households on the horizontal axis. It always starts at (0%, 0%) and ends at (100%, 100%). If every household had the exact same income, the lowest-earning x% of households would always receive x% of total income, tracing the straight 45-degree diagonal called the line of equality. When incomes differ, lower-income groups receive smaller shares than higher-income groups, so the Lorenz curve bows below the line of equality and grows steeper from left to right. The further it sags below the diagonal, the more unequal the distribution.

To summarise the diagram in one number, write both axes as proportions from 0 to 1 instead of percentages, so the whole square has area 1 and the triangle beneath the line of equality has area 0.5. Let A be the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve, and let B be the area beneath the Lorenz curve. Since A + B = 0.5, the Gini coefficient G is defined as

When everyone earns the same, A = 0 and G = 0. At the opposite extreme, in a large population where a single household receives all income and every other household receives nothing, B shrinks towards 0 and G approaches 1. When a Lorenz curve is drawn with straight segments between group boundaries, B is the sum of the areas under those segments, where a strip of width w rising from height h₁ to h₂ has area
strip area = w × (h₁ + h₂) ÷ 2

Because both axes measure shares of totals, multiplying every household's income by the same positive factor leaves the Lorenz curve and G unchanged, and neither tells how high average income is. Moreover, two distributions whose Lorenz curves cross can enclose the same total area A and therefore share the same Gini coefficient. Figure 1 shows the piecewise-linear Lorenz curve of one region.

blocks.text: Computers store and transmit text by encoding each character as a binary codeword, a sequence of bits written 0 and 1. In a fixed-length code every character uses the same number of bits, k. Because k bits can form 2^k different patterns, an alphabet of m characters needs the smallest integer k with 2^k ≥ m: two bits distinguish at most four characters, while five to eight characters need three bits each.

Text can often be stored in fewer bits with a variable-length code, which gives short codewords to common characters and longer codewords to rare ones. Variable lengths create a risk when codewords are joined end to end without spaces. Suppose X were encoded as 0, Y as 1 and Z as 01: the bit string 01 could then mean either "X followed by Y" or "Z alone". A code avoids this ambiguity if it is prefix-free (also called a prefix code): no codeword in the code is an initial segment, or prefix, of any other codeword. When a code is prefix-free, a receiver reading from left to right recognises the end of each codeword the instant a valid codeword is completed, with no separator needed.

Every binary prefix-free code can be drawn as a binary code tree starting from a root on the left (Figure 1). Each branching point, or internal node, splits into an upper branch labelled 0 and a lower branch labelled 1. Characters are placed only at the leaves, the endpoints with no branches leaving them; that rule ensures no character's path is the start of another's. A character's codeword is the sequence of branch bits from the root to its leaf, so its length in bits equals the number of steps from the root.

blocks.text: Whether researchers weigh a chemical sample or test verbal reasoning, every measurement tries to capture an underlying value or attribute. In practice, single readings depart from the true value because of two distinct kinds of measurement error. Random error consists of unpredictable chance fluctuations from one occasion, item or observer to the next — a momentary lapse of attention, a lucky guess on one multiple-choice item, or slight timing noise. Because random errors push readings up and down without a fixed direction, they tend to cancel out when many items or repeated readings are averaged. Systematic error, or bias, pushes measurements consistently in the same direction every time, like a weighing scale whose zero mark is offset by fifty grams, or an arithmetic test written in needlessly dense prose that penalises second-language readers every time they sit it.

Reliability is the consistency of a measurement when the attribute being measured has not changed. Researchers check it in several ways. Test–retest reliability asks whether giving the same instrument to the same people on two occasions yields close scores. Parallel-forms reliability asks whether two equivalent versions of a test produce matching results. Inter-rater reliability asks whether independent observers scoring the same performance agree with one another. Random error is the main enemy of reliability: the larger the random noise, the more scores jump around from trial to trial.

Validity, by contrast, asks whether an instrument actually measures what it claims to measure rather than something else. In the social sciences many targets — such as working memory, job satisfaction or civic trust — are constructs, abstract theoretical concepts that cannot be seen directly. Construct validity concerns how faithfully the chosen tasks or questions reflect that target construct rather than an irrelevant skill such as reading speed. Criterion validity checks how closely scores match an external benchmark, called the criterion: it is concurrent validity when the measure and the criterion are recorded at the same time, and predictive validity when today's score is checked against an outcome measured later.

Reliability and validity are linked in one direction only. A measure can be highly reliable without being valid: systematic error leaves repeated readings tightly clustered around the wrong value or the wrong trait. Yet a measure that has no reliability cannot be valid: if scores are swamped by random error and agree neither across occasions nor across raters, they cannot accurately track the intended attribute either.

blocks.text: When people disagree about what someone ought to do, they often appeal to two different moral standards: the outcomes an action brings about, or the duties and rights the action respects. In moral philosophy these two standards are developed systematically as act-consequentialism and deontological ethics.

Consequentialism holds that whether an action is morally right or wrong depends solely on its consequences — the states of affairs that follow from it — rather than on the intrinsic kind of act it is or on commitments made beforehand. Under act-consequentialism, an agent facing a choice ought to perform whichever available action produces the greatest net balance of good over bad outcomes overall. In its best-known version, classic utilitarianism, good is understood as well-being, and every affected person's gain or loss counts impartially, meaning equally regardless of who performs the act or how they are connected to the agent. Because only the net sum of consequences matters, no type of action — such as breaking a promise or withholding the truth — is ruled out in advance if, in that particular case, doing so produces a better total outcome than every alternative.

Deontological ethics, named from the Greek word deon ("duty"), denies that outcomes are the whole story. It holds that certain kinds of choice are intrinsically required, permitted or forbidden by moral duties and individual rights, even when breaking a duty would yield a somewhat larger total of good results. Philosophers in this tradition, notably Immanuel Kant, emphasise moral constraints against using people merely as a means — as tools for advancing a broader goal without regard for their own consent or rights. Many deontological theories also recognise agent-centred duties: special obligations an agent owes to particular people because of a prior promise, contract or role, which cannot simply be set aside whenever strangers would gain slightly more.

In everyday life the two frameworks often recommend the very same outward action, for instance honouring an agreement when doing so both keeps a promise and preserves useful cooperation. Even then, their underlying reasons differ: the consequentialist points to the future benefits of mutual trust, whereas the deontologist points to the obligation created by the agreement itself. Their verdicts pull apart in conflict cases where keeping a moral constraint, such as truthfulness or promise-keeping, produces a smaller net total of good outcomes than breaking it, or where achieving a wider benefit requires imposing an unconsented burden on one person.

options.text: Whether the action produces a greater net balance of good over bad outcomes overall than any available alternative.
options.why: This states the definition of act-consequentialism in the second paragraph.

options.text: Whether the action benefits the agent's close associates more than it benefits strangers.
options.why: Act-consequentialism in its classic utilitarian form counts everyone's good impartially rather than favouring close associates.

questions.stem: According to the text, what determines whether an action is morally right under act-consequentialism?

questions.explanation: Opening the folder 2 years early would raise total net benefit slightly without harming the donor, so act-consequentialism would favour opening it. Refusing solely because a binding promise was made illustrates deontological (duty-based) reasoning.

options.text: Impartial utilitarianism, because the archivist weighs the botanist's comfort more heavily than the researchers' time.
options.why: The scenario states the botanist would suffer no distress, and the archivist appeals to the promise itself rather than weighing comfort.

options.text: Act-consequentialism, because keeping the folder sealed produces the largest total time saving across everyone involved.
options.why: Keeping the folder sealed forfeits the time saving for the 15 researchers without creating a larger gain elsewhere.

options.text: Outcome maximisation, because the archivist judges the choice exclusively by the states of affairs that follow from it.
options.why: Looking back to a prior promise rather than forward to net outcomes is the opposite of outcome maximisation.

options.text: Deontological ethics, because a duty arising from a prior promise constrains the choice even when breaking it would raise net benefit.
options.why: Refusing to break a promise despite a modest net gain in outcomes exemplifies a deontological constraint.

questions.stem: A university archivist promised a retiring botanist to keep a folder of harmless personal field diaries sealed for 10 years. Opening the folder 2 years early would modestly save time for 15 visiting researchers and cause the botanist no distress, yet the archivist refuses solely on the ground that a promise was given. Which ethical approach does the archivist's reasoning illustrate?

questions.explanation: The board aggregates lost water hours impartially across all 4,000 homes and chooses the option with the best net outcome even though it breaks a prior written assurance to 30 homes. That directly reflects impartial act-consequentialism.

options.text: Act-consequentialism, counting every household's disruption impartially and letting the best net outcome override the prior assurance.
options.why: Minimising total disruption across all households equally, even at the cost of breaking a prior promise, applies impartial act-consequentialism.

options.text: Deontological ethics, upholding an agent-centred duty owed specifically to the thirty households that received the written assurance.
options.why: An agent-centred duty to those thirty households would speak against breaking the written assurance given to them.

options.text: Kant's constraint against using a smaller group's inconvenience as a means to reduce inconvenience for a larger group.
options.why: That constraint would forbid overriding the assurance to the thirty households merely to lower the city-wide total.

options.text: A rule that treats every category of promise-breaking as unconditionally forbidden whatever the size of the disruption saved.
options.why: The board explicitly breaks its written assurance to secure fewer lost hours overall, rejecting an unconditional prohibition.

questions.stem: A municipal water board must choose between two pipe-repair schedules across 4,000 homes. It calculates total hours without tap water across all 4,000 homes, counting every household's hour equally, and picks the schedule with the fewest total hours lost even though doing so breaks an earlier written assurance given to 30 homes on one street. Which framework from the text guides this decision?

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph explains that both frameworks frequently recommend the same outward act (such as keeping an agreement that also sustains cooperation) for different underlying reasons, while pulling apart when keeping a moral constraint yields less overall good than breaking it.

options.text: The two frameworks must recommend opposite outward actions in every situation, because one looks to outcomes and the other to duties.
options.why: The fourth paragraph explicitly notes that in everyday life both frameworks often recommend the same outward action for different reasons.

options.text: Deontological ethics ignores individual rights altogether, whereas act-consequentialism treats individual rights as unbreakable limits on action.
options.why: This swaps the two views: deontological ethics treats duties and rights as constraints, while act-consequentialism allows any act that maximises net good.

options.text: Both frameworks can endorse the same outward action for different reasons, and diverge when respecting a moral constraint lowers total net good.
options.why: This summarises the fourth paragraph on everyday convergence of actions alongside divergence in reasons and conflict cases.

options.text: Act-consequentialism gives extra weight to promises made by the agent, whereas deontological ethics counts only impartial well-being.
options.why: Special obligations from an agent's own promises belong to agent-centred deontology, whereas impartial well-being belongs to utilitarianism.

questions.stem: Which statement accurately describes how act-consequentialism and deontological ethics compare according to the text?

questions.explanation: Under act-consequentialism, promise-breaking was opposed at first only because of its bad ripple effects on trust; once those negative consequences vanish and the pantry donation produces greater net good, act-consequentialism favours donating. Under deontological ethics, the duty created by the promise to repay binds even when breaking it yields more net good.

options.text: Both frameworks shift to recommending the donation, because neither counts a promise once wider trust is unaffected.
options.why: Deontological promise-keeping rests on the duty owed to the promisee, not solely on indirect effects on public trust.

options.text: Act-consequentialism shifts to recommending the donation, whereas deontological ethics continues to require repaying the neighbour.
options.why: With indirect trust losses removed, donating maximises net good, whereas the duty to keep a promise still binds deontologically.

options.text: Deontological ethics shifts to recommending the donation, whereas act-consequentialism continues to require repaying the neighbour.
options.why: This reverses the two theories: removing negative consequences shifts the outcome-based verdict, not the duty-based constraint.

options.text: Neither framework changes its verdict, because act-consequentialism forbids breaking a debt agreement regardless of the outcomes.
options.why: The second paragraph notes that act-consequentialism never rules out breaking a promise in advance when doing so yields a better total outcome.

questions.stem: Suppose a borrower owes €200 today to a prosperous neighbour who would not miss the money, while donating that €200 to a local food pantry today would create a larger direct gain in well-being. At first, both an act-consequentialist and a deontologist advise repaying the neighbour: the act-consequentialist because public default would damage wider neighbourhood trust, and the deontologist because the borrower promised to repay. Suppose the situation changes so that donating instead of repaying would remain completely unknown to others and cause no wider loss of trust. How do the verdicts of the two frameworks change?

questions.explanation: Both editors vote the same way, illustrating the fourth paragraph's point that outward verdicts can agree while reasons differ. Editor P weighs future harms (wasted purchases, lost subscriptions) against immediate sales gains — act-consequentialist reasoning. Editor Q appeals to a duty not to deceive and not to treat readers merely as a means, explicitly independent of consequences — deontological reasoning.

options.text: Both P and Q rely on act-consequentialist reasoning, because both editors reach the exact same vote against publishing the table.
options.why: The fourth paragraph stresses that reaching the same outward decision does not mean sharing the same ethical reasoning.

options.text: Both P and Q rely on deontological reasoning, because both editors oppose boosting the magazine's own sales.
options.why: Editor P opposes publication by weighing long-run net outcomes across buyers and subscriptions, which is consequentialist reasoning.

options.text: P relies on deontological reasoning about reader trust, whereas Q relies on act-consequentialist reasoning about circulation.
options.why: P weighs total future harms against short-term sales (consequentialism), whereas Q invokes an unconditional duty not to deceive or use readers merely as means (deontology).

options.text: They reach the same outward decision from opposite frameworks: P argues on act-consequentialist grounds and Q on deontological grounds.
options.why: P compares net long-run consequences, while Q appeals to a constraint against deception and using readers merely as a means regardless of detection.

questions.stem: Two editors at a consumer magazine both vote against publishing unverified battery-life figures that would boost this month's sales. Editor P argues: "Once buyers find that real battery life falls short of our table, cancelled subscriptions and wasted purchases will outweigh this month's extra sales." Editor Q argues: "Printing figures we know are unverified deceives readers and uses them merely as instruments to lift circulation, which is wrong even if nobody ever checks our table." How does the text classify P's and Q's arguments?
